transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
President Trump heads to Asia this week for two meetings.
First, he stops in the Philippines to talk trade and security with Southeast Asian leaders.
Then he heads to China for a historic meeting with President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin.
Airlines are working to get a backlog of passengers back up in planes after Friday's nationwide ground stop.
Trump administration officials say it's up to Congress to approve more money to fix outdated technology,
as NPR's Mara Liasson reports.
Speaking to reporters yesterday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said communication systems work by a contractor was the culprit,
not new AI tools or a cyber attack.
We don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment.
Duffy blamed Congress for not giving the FAA more money for upgrades,
but Republicans who are still in charge of Congress until January already approved $12.5 billion for safety upgrades in the one big beautiful bill.
Democrats on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee say that the administration has only spent $1 billion of those funds.
Mara Liasson, NPR News.
As Democrats get ready to take control of both chambers of Congress in January,
there's competition for who will be majority leader of the Senate.
Current minority leader Chuck Schumer, who had the majority role from 2021 to 2025 before Republicans took control, plans to run again.
But Senator Chris Van Hollen also wants the job.
This is not about one person or any one individual.
This really is a response to the call of the voters who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies.
But they haven't fully hired the Democrats.
They've given us a chance.
And I think we need to earn their trust.
And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.
Speaking there on CNN's State of the Union.
Ukraine says Russian attacks killed four people and injured dozens of others across Ukraine over the past day.
And here's Eleanor Beardsley reports.
Air raid sirens went off throughout Sunday in Kiev and other cities across the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs,
and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week.
He said continued restrictions on the speed of Star Shield, the militarized version of Starlink,
are preventing Ukrainian interceptor drones from taking down jet-powered Shahid drones.
Russian forces are targeting energy substations with the Shahid drones.
Zelensky said many of the strikes get through precisely because speed restrictions remain in place.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kyiv.
You're listening to NPR News.
Some Americans squeezed by high prices are turning to local libraries to save money.
And here's Joe Hernandez reports.
Several large U.S. public libraries are seeing an increase in card holders, circulation, and attendance at events.
At the Chicago Public Library, visits, adult library card applications, and Wi-Fi sessions were all up in the first seven months of this year.
The library streaming app Canopy reported a 41 percent spike in users last year alone.
Samantha Mears, a spokesperson for the Maricopa County Library District in Arizona,
says they've seen recent upticks in card holders and digital media use and more people using the library's services.
You can see in times of economic hardship, we have more people coming and reaching out to us.
Of course, it's not just the cost of living that's a factor.
Librarians say they're getting better at marketing themselves to the public and that the pandemic lockdowns accelerated the adoption of digital media like e-books.
Joe Hernandez, NPR News.
A Georgia O'Keefe painting found buried behind coats and boxes in the closet of an apartment building in Manhattan for decades is heading to the auction block.
The painting was found in the home of a woman in her 90s who died recently.
Christie's estimates the painting depicting a classic New Mexico landscape with rolling hills and earth tones will go for between three to five million dollars.
The auction house says the painting is from 1930 and is probably the first in a series of three.
The second is at the New York Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The other was in the Rockefeller Family Collection.
You're listening to NPR News.

topics.text: Trump heads to Philippines, then China for meetings with Xi Jinping and Putin
Airlines work to clear passenger backlog after Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop
Duffy blames Congress for underfunding FAA upgrades; Democrats say only $1 billion spent
Schumer and Van Hollen compete for Senate majority leader role in Democratic-led Congress
Russian attacks kill four and injure dozens across Ukraine over the past day
Americans squeezed by high prices turn to public libraries, with card sign-ups and usage rising
Georgia O'Keeffe painting found hidden in Manhattan apartment closet heads to auction
